newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: SNB nudges rates lower to halt Swiss franc gains.
newsitem.headline: SNB nudges rates lower to halt Swiss franc gains.

text.p: The Swiss National Bank added liquidity to the money market, following its statement on Wednesday that it would react to the Swiss franc's gains with a "significant expansion" of liquidity.

Traders said the SNB added liquidity to the money market at lower than usual rates this morning. One bank said the SNB lowered the rate on its routine liquidity operations to 1-3/8 percent from the 1-5/8 percent seen recently.
But the SNB itself says it does not target any particular money market rate, and a spokesman declined comment on the operations.
The SNB, in its regular 10-day statement, also said that Swiss sight deposits rose by 724.7 million Swiss francs to 4.33 billion in the reporting period ended May 20, a large increase.
"We have put additional liquidity in the market to underscore our statement," an SNB spokesman said.

One money market trader believed the SNB had not deviated from its generous policy. It began lowering the discount rate from a peak of seven percent in 1991, to one percent today. It actions were stepped up as the Swiss franc appreciated amidst tension in the run-up to European Economic and Monetary Union.
The one percent discount rate currently matches the historic low maintained from February 1978 to November 1979.
"You can say they might be easing. But they have kept to an easier policy," the trader said.
Money market traders said that the SNB appeared to be especially aggressive in its operations on Wednesday.
"They want to show that they really mean business," said one.

The Swiss franc also tumbled against the mark and dollar. The mark is seen as the key currency for Swiss trade. It recently hit seven-month lows versus the franc. This morning it traded back above 83.00 Swiss centimes, up from the opening of 82.70.
The SNB's statement, released with its 10-day reserves statement, also showed it would continue to work to stop any unwanted franc appreciation.
"The SNB has said repeatedly that it would work against any unrealistic appreciation of the Swiss franc caused by developments in European currencies," it said.
"In the most recent past, the upwards pressure lacked any fundamental basis. The SNB has thus reacted with a significant increase in liqudiity.
"This policy will be consequently continued," the SNB said in its statement.
